lessons.title: Selecting suitable seed growers
lessons.html:
Selecting suitable seed growers

Most seed companies do not farm all their seed themselves. They contract farmers, called seed growers, to produce seed crops on their land under the company's supervision. Choosing the right growers is one of the most important decisions in seed production, because a poor grower can produce seed that fails certification and causes losses for both parties.

What makes a good seed grower?

  • Suitable land and climate for the crop, for example irrigated land in the Northern Cape or Free State for hybrid maize seed, or suitable areas for wheat or soybean seed.
  • Isolation from other fields of the same crop, as required for the seed class.
  • Reliable irrigation where needed, with enough water rights in terms of the National Water Act 36 of 1998.
  • Management skill and willingness to follow the company's instructions, such as detasselling and roguing.
  • Equipment such as planters, sprayers and harvesters that can be cleaned between crops.
  • Labour for tasks like detasselling.
  • Track record and good financial standing.

Assessing a grower

  1. Visit the farm and inspect the proposed fields and surroundings.
  2. Check field history: previous crops, volunteer problems, weeds, soil problems.
  3. Discuss the requirements and the grower's experience.
  4. Check references and past performance with the company.
  5. Record the assessment and recommend to your manager.

Planning quantities

The company's production plan sets how much seed of each cultivar is needed. Divide the needed hectares between growers to spread risk from hail, drought or disease. Do not depend on a single grower for an important cultivar.

lessons.title: The seed production contract
lessons.html:
The seed production contract

Once a grower is selected, a written contract sets out what each party must do. A clear contract prevents disputes later, for example about payment for seed that did not pass quality standards.

Typical contract contents

SectionContent
Parties and fieldsNames, farm, field numbers, hectares
Crop and cultivarIncluding class and parent seed supplied
Grower obligationsFollow production instructions, isolation, detasselling, roguing, allow inspections, keep records
Company obligationsSupply parent seed, technical advice, inspections, harvest scheduling
Quality standardsCertification, purity, germination, moisture at delivery
DeliveryWhere, when and how seed is delivered
PaymentPrice basis, premiums, deductions, payment dates
Ownership and confidentialityParent seed and harvested seed belong to the company; grower may not keep or sell it
Risk and disputesWhat happens with crop failure, rejection, and how disputes are resolved

Explaining the contract

Go through the contract with the grower before signing. Make sure they understand the obligations, especially that parent seed and the seed crop are the company's property and protected by plant breeders' rights. Answer questions and check that the person signing has authority to sign for the farming business.

Signing and records

  • Both parties sign and date the contract. Each keeps a copy.
  • Register the fields for certification with the authority where required.
  • Record the contract in the company's grower database.

Managing the relationship

Visit growers during the season, give technical support, communicate inspection results promptly and pay on time. Good growers are hard to find; treat them as partners.

Key points

  • Select growers for land, isolation, water, skill, equipment and track record.
  • Spread production across several growers to reduce risk.
  • Put obligations, standards, delivery and payment in a written contract.
  • Parent and harvested seed belong to the company and may not be kept or sold.
  • Support growers and pay on time to build lasting partnerships.
